subtopics.title: Complement of an event set
subtopics.exposition: The complement of a set A is a new set that contains all of the elements that are not in A. Since every element in the sample space is either in A or in A', the union of complementary events covers the sample space. The union of an event A and its complement A' is the sample space: A ∪ A' = S. The complement of A is written A', or sometimes not(A).

subtopics.title: Mutually exclusive events
subtopics.exposition: Since every element in A is not in A', complementary events are mutually exclusive. The intersection of an event A and its complement A' is the empty set: A ∩ A' = ∅. To decide whether two events are mutually exclusive, look at their intersection: if the intersection A ∩ B is not empty, the events are not mutually exclusive.

subtopics.title: Probability of a complement
subtopics.exposition: From A ∩ A' = ∅ and A ∪ A' = S, the probabilities of complementary events sum to 1. P(A) + P(A') = P(A ∪ A') = P(S) = 1.

subtopics.title: Venn diagram region counts
subtopics.exposition: The identity for the union of two events: P(A ∪ B) = P(A) + P(B) - P(A ∩ B). To reason with a Venn diagram, first summarise the sizes of the sample space, the event sets, their union and their intersection. The number of elements in the union of the two events is the size of the sample space minus the number in neither event: 70 - 15 = 55 people use at least one product, so n(A ∪ B) = 55. When the size of the intersection of the two events is not given, work out n(A ∩ B) by using the identity for the union of two events. Rewrite the union identity in terms of numbers of elements by writing each probability as the number of elements in the event divided by n(S): n(A ∪ B)/n(S) = n(A)/n(S) + n(B)/n(S) - n(A ∩ B)/n(S). Substitute the known counts and solve for the intersection: n(A ∩ B) = 25 + 35 - 55 = 5. Events that are not mutually exclusive have circles that overlap in the Venn diagram. Draw the Venn diagram and fill in the numbers. Read off the answers from the Venn diagram: the number who use A only, B only, and both (20, 30 and 5 in the example). The size of the sample space is written n(S), and it equals the number of people questioned in the survey (n(S) = 70 in the example).

claims.claim: The complement of a set A is a new set that contains all of the elements that are not in A.
The complement of A is written A', or sometimes not(A).
Since every element in A is not in A', complementary events are mutually exclusive.
The intersection of an event A and its complement A' is the empty set: A ∩ A' = ∅.
Since every element in the sample space is either in A or in A', the union of complementary events covers the sample space.
The union of an event A and its complement A' is the sample space: A ∪ A' = S.
From A ∩ A' = ∅ and A ∪ A' = S, the probabilities of complementary events sum to 1.
To reason with a Venn diagram, first summarise the sizes of the sample space, the event sets, their union and their intersection.

When the size of the intersection of the two events is not given, work out n(A ∩ B) by using the identity for the union of two events.
The identity for the union of two events: P(A ∪ B) = P(A) + P(B) - P(A ∩ B).
Rewrite the union identity in terms of numbers of elements by writing each probability as the number of elements in the event divided by n(S): n(A ∪ B)/n(S) = n(A)/n(S) + n(B)/n(S) - n(A ∩ B)/n(S).
Substitute the known counts and solve for the intersection: n(A ∩ B) = 25 + 35 - 55 = 5.
To decide whether two events are mutually exclusive, look at their intersection: if the intersection A ∩ B is not empty, the events are not mutually exclusive.
Events that are not mutually exclusive have circles that overlap in the Venn diagram.
Draw the Venn diagram and fill in the numbers.
Read off the answers from the Venn diagram: the number who use A only, B only, and both (20, 30 and 5 in the example).
